archetype.name: Bubble Team (outshot, PP-reliant)
archetype.definition: Winnipeg is a team near .500 whose November surge pulled it back into the race, but whose 5-on-5 play still sits in the league's bottom third and closely matches last year's 82-point team.

report.headline: November's goal binge rescued the record; the shot share says it's still a bubble team
report.take:
The Jets are two seasons removed from finishing first on this site with 116 points, and one removed from an 82-point slide. At 11-9-4 they sit seventh in the Central, ahead of only Chicago, and 21st on the site. The record looks like a recovery. The underlying play looks like last season. Their 5-on-5 expected-goals share is .479 this year against .478 a year ago, and their shot-attempt share has dipped to .48. This is the same team in better form, not a fixed one.

The swing came from offense. October was a 4-10 hole built on 2.43 goals a game. November has been a 7-3 month at 4.1 goals a game, including an 8-3 rout in Dallas and a 6-2 win over Vancouver inside a six-game winning streak. The defense did not come along. Over the last ten games they allowed 3.5 a game, slightly worse than their season rate, and over the full season they give up 31.6 shots a game, the most in the league. The power play, 10th at 23.9%, is the one structural upgrade. It is well ahead of last year's 18.5% and gives a thin lineup a real way to score.

The numbers hide two things. First, the goaltending is not the problem it looks like. A combined .883 save percentage ranks 26th, but team GSAx is basically even at 0.3, and Stuart Skinner is slightly positive at 1.0 despite that .883. He is facing a lot of shots, and dangerous ones. Second, the blueline is leaking at a rate nobody else matches. Opposing defensemen score more against Winnipeg than against any team, 0.7 points a game against an expected 0.39, and they account for more than half the points the Jets allow. Forwards are held well under expectation, so the damage comes from point shots and pinches the structure doesn't handle.

Where it goes: the pace is 89 points, which in 2021-22 was a 19th-place team. With D- grades for both the forwards and the blueline, a 24th-ranked penalty kill and the league's heaviest shot load, the November scoring is more likely to cool than the defense is to tighten. Expect the record to drift back toward its goal differential: a fringe team chasing a wild card rather than holding one.

strengths.title: A power play that can carry nights
strengths.body: At 23.9% the power play ranks 10th and sits above the league average. That is a clear jump from last season's 18.5%. It is the most reliable source of offense for a roster whose forward group grades D-, and special-teams rates this far into a season are usually more stable than 5-on-5 shooting.

strengths.title: Goaltending holding level under siege
strengths.body: The save percentage looks bad, but goalies GSAx is essentially neutral at 0.3, 15th in the league. Skinner is slightly above expected while facing the league's heaviest shot volume. The goalies are mostly stopping what an average goalie would, so the goals against are a team-defense problem. That should hold as long as the workload doesn't wear them down.

concerns.title: Outshot and out-chanced at 5-on-5
concerns.body: The Jets allow 31.6 shots a game, last in the league, and hold only a .479 share of 5-on-5 expected goals (23rd). That share is nearly identical to last season's 82-point team, so this is not a slump. It is the team's baseline, and the November win streak didn't change it.

concerns.title: Defensemen-driven leaks and a weak kill
concerns.body: Opposing defensemen produce 0.7 points a game against Winnipeg, the worst mark in the league, and supply over half of all points allowed against a league norm under a third. Add a 72.5% penalty kill (24th) and the Jets give away goals in two ways that compound each other. The D- blueline grade suggests personnel, not bad luck.

concerns.title: Hot streak built on scoring, not stops
concerns.body: November's 4.1 goals a game drove the 7-3 month, while goals allowed rose to 3.5 a game. Over the last ten, scoring is up nearly a goal a game on the season while goals allowed got slightly worse. Several of those wins came in overtime. When the scoring cools, nothing behind it holds the record up.

trend.note: A nine-game losing streak sank October, then a six-game winning streak turned November into a 7-3 month. Since the streak ended they have alternated, and the one-goal and overtime games are piling up.

weekAhead.headline: Three road games against top-ten teams, bookended by Utah and Chicago
weekAhead.body:
Five games in eight days, and the middle of it is the hard part. After hosting Utah, the Jets go to Boston (3rd on the site), then play the Islanders and Devils on back-to-back nights. Boston and the Islanders have two of the league's best goaltending tandems, which is exactly the matchup that cools an offense riding its finishing. New Jersey and Utah both drive play far better than Winnipeg does, but both have weak goaltending and leaky penalty kills.

The Jets have already beaten the Devils, Islanders and Blackhawks this month, two of those in overtime or one-goal games. A Chicago team ranked 31st, among the worst in the league at driving play, closes the week at home. Taking points from the bookends and stealing one on the road would be a solid week. Their own shot-share profile makes a losing road swing the likelier script.

keyMatchups.title: Winnipeg PK vs Utah's power play
keyMatchups.body: Utah converts 32.5% of its power plays, third in the league, against a Jets kill that ranks 24th. Utah's poor goaltending (GSAx -10.3) gives the Jets an opening at the other end. In a home game they should want, avoiding the penalty box decides it.

keyMatchups.title: Hot offense meets elite goalies
keyMatchups.body: Boston's goalies are at +11.7 GSAx and the Islanders' at +13.4, both with a .910 save percentage. Winnipeg's November scoring has outrun its chance share, and these are the goalies who make that kind of team pay. Expect low-event, low-scoring road games.

keyMatchups.title: Jets power play vs Devils' kill
keyMatchups.body: New Jersey kills only 64.2% of penalties, 30th in the league, and its goalies sit at -9.4 GSAx. The Devils control play at 5-on-5 (CF % .56), so Winnipeg's best route on the second night of a back-to-back is drawing penalties for a top-ten power play.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the shots-against load drops in the Boston-Islanders-Devils road stretch. If Skinner faces 30-plus a night again, the November form is on borrowed time.

restOfSeason.body:
The current pace is 38 wins and 89 points with a -24 differential. That is the pace of a team just outside the playoff cut, and it already includes a month of scoring well above anything the shot share supports. The repeatable parts are a top-ten power play and goaltending that is roughly average against heavy volume. The parts likely to fade are the 4-plus goals a game in November and some of the overtime results. A 5-on-5 profile nearly identical to last year's says this team lands near last year's level, a little better thanks to the power play.

My expectation is 80 to 88 points and 33 to 38 wins, with goals allowed staying stubbornly above three a game unless the blueline improves. The upside case needs the penalty kill to climb toward league average and the defensemen to stop feeding opponents' points. Neither is visible in the sheet yet.
swingFactors: Penalty kill recovering toward league average
Whether the power play keeps converting above 23%

confidence.note: 24 games is a modest sample, but the 5-on-5 numbers match last season's, which firms up the read.
